source.title: World Engine: Towards the Era of Post-Training for Autonomous Driving
source.authors: Tianyu Li; Li Chen; Cao-Jun Wang; Hao-Chen Liu; Kashyap Chitta; Z. Yang; Yu-Hang Lu; Nai-Sheng Ye; Yi-Hang Qiu; Yu-Fei Wang; Lu-Lu Zou; Jia Peng; Jin Pan; Zhao-Yu Su; Andrei Bursuc; S. Li; Andreas Geiger; Peng Su; Hong-Yang Li

record.tranche_reason: The paper mentions language-model pre-training as context and cites Kaplan et al., but it does not test or rely on the claimed language-model loss laws. Its own scaling experiments concern autonomous-driving models and task metrics.
record.gate_note: The paper reports an autonomous-driving data-scaling experiment, not held-out language-model cross-entropy, power-law fits, or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. Its scaling results are recorded as related findings with versions ["none"].
record.test_reason: The study cites Kaplan et al. only as background on LLM pre-training. Its own scaling experiment varies driving pre-training data from 12k to 103k scenes for a single 58.3M-parameter driving policy. It reports driving-task scores (open-loop PDMS, closed-loop success rate), not held-out loss. No power-law fit or exponent is reported, and parameters and compute are not varied. None of V1–V7 is tested. V5 names the power-law form of loss in other modalities, and V6 names language-model downstream predictability, so neither applies.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is correct. The authors conclude that RL post-training on synthesized rare driving events improves safety more data-efficiently than scaling passive pre-training data, matching gains of about 10× more data. They draw no conclusions about language-model scaling laws.
record.recipe_differences: The study varies autonomous-driving pre-training data and measures driving-task metrics; it does not reproduce the language-model loss measurements or compute-allocation analyses.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports different scaling behavior for common and rare driving cases: common-case performance improves predictably, while rare-case gains saturate.

fits_no_version.finding: For a 58.3M end-to-end driving policy, common-case open-loop PDMS improves steadily as pre-training data grows from 12k to 103k scenes. Rare-case open-loop PDMS and closed-loop success rate gains saturate.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In autonomous driving, task performance on rare safety-critical cases scales more weakly with pre-training data than performance on common cases.

fits_no_version.finding: The authors extrapolate the data-scaling curve and say pre-training alone would need roughly 10× (Fig. 2 caption: ~14×) more data to match the closed-loop gains from post-training. The functional form used for this extrapolation is not stated.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Targeted post-training can match gains that extrapolated pre-training data scaling would reach only with about an order of magnitude more data.

record.problems: The related scaling results concern autonomous-driving task metrics and are described qualitatively here; the paper does not report language-model loss measurements, fitted exponents, or compute-optimal allocation results.

untested.parts: Language-model held-out loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
Extrapolation of loss fits from small to much larger runs.
Compute-optimal split between parameters and tokens.
Effect of architecture shape on loss at a fixed parameter count.
Power-law loss form in other modalities. Driving loss is not measured and no power law is fitted.
Downstream predictability from language-model scale or loss.
Dependence of fitted exponents on setup and fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: The scaling curve is reported only in Figure 2a, with no numbers in the text and no fitted functional form. The extrapolation multiple differs between the text (~10×) and the Fig. 2 caption (~14×).

versions.untested_parts: Language-model held-out loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute.
Extrapolation of language-model loss from small to much larger runs.
Architecture effects on language-model loss at fixed parameter count.
The study does not test whether the same power-law form holds beyond text pretraining.
Downstream predictability from language-model scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of language-model exponents or compute-optimal allocation on fitting and setup choices.
